item.title: NorCal Emergency Repeaters: Which Machines Stay Up When Things Go Sideways
item.description:
When the power goes out and the cell towers go quiet, every ham asks the same question: which repeater do I reach for?

Not the closest one. Not the one with the clever callsign. The one most likely to still be on the air. The one sitting on a mountaintop with batteries, run by a club that actually shows up, and written into the county’s emergency plan.

So I built a tool to find out. It’s part of a project I call RadioBuilder, and this is its first public output. For each of 8 regions, from the Bay Area to the Eastern Sierra, it pulls repeater listings, checks FCC license records, looks up the true elevation of each site with the USGS, and layers in research on who runs the machine, when their nets meet, and whether a county ARES, RACES or CERT plan names it. item.title: Room Servers for Emergency Communications: Building Resilient Infrastructure
item.description:
When the cell towers go down—and they will, eventually—most people lose their ability to communicate. No 911. No texting family. No calling for help. Just silence.

But if you’ve built mesh infrastructure with room servers, you have something that works regardless of cellular, internet, or power grid status. That’s not theoretical capability. That’s actual resilience.

Why Room Servers Matter for Emergency Response

In a disaster scenario:

Cellular infrastructure is first to fail. Cell towers have backup power measured in hours. Data centers have days. Your mesh network with room server infrastructure has as much uptime as you engineered it to have.
